comments.text:
I visited Xinjiang in 1995 as part of my Silk Road Journey (started in Beijing), at that time, the only modern city in this Autonomous Administrative Region was Urumqi, built with many high rise edifices.  The Han population was also prevalent and Muslim women at that time did not have their head covered, at least it was not something that I had noticed.

Xinjiang is China’s New El Dorado in the 21st C., not only because it is at the crossroads of the Belt & Road Initiative Project, but it is also China’s economic, industrial, technological, agricultural, minerals, renewable energy and AI data centers development bastion of the Country’s Northwestern regions.  

Given the upcoming retirement of farmers (baby boomers generation) in Han-populated areas of the country , the aging population as well as the low birth rate, Xinjiang is becoming the granary and major food supply chain of the country due to the availability of large flat lands, which can accommodate mechanization, AI-assisted robotization for large-scale agricultural activities/production.  Further, cheap renewable energy production (solar and wind) as well as aquaculture production constitute Xinjiang’s major assets in addition to its ideal AI data centers location.  The South-West Water Diversion  Project  from the Tibet/QingHai Plateau to Xinjiang known as the Red Flag Water Project is being built currently, which would resolve the water scarcity problems in the northeastern regions.  Further, Chinese geologists have even found aquifers under the deserts of Xinjiang lately.

comments.author: @tonywong2204
comments.text:
这部纪录片是我见过最懂新疆的镜头。它没有用炫技的运镜去喧宾夺主，而是把每一帧都交还给了这片土地本身 —— 天山雪峰在晨光里泛着淡蓝的冷光，帕米尔高原的云层贴着山脊流动，喀纳斯的湖水绿得让人屏息，沙漠的曲线在黄昏里被拉成柔软的金色。航拍俯瞰时，山河的壮阔扑面而来；镜头拉近，牧民转场时驼铃的响动、胡杨林里漏下的光斑、赛里木湖畔一朵不知名的野花，全都带着真实而鲜活的温度。
最打动我的是它不着急、不喧闹的叙事节奏。风声、雪融声、马蹄踏过草甸的声音，被原原本本收进了画面，仿佛把人也带到了那片辽阔的天地之间。它拍的不只是风景，更是一种人与自然之间从容共处的状态 —— 那份辽阔与宁静，透过屏幕也能让人心里静下来。
看完只有一个念头：新疆的美，值得被这样认真、温柔地记录。这部纪录片做到了。

This documentary is the most perceptive lens through which I have ever beheld Xinjiang.
It does not hijack the frame with showmanship; it returns every single frame to the land itself. The snow-capped peaks of the Tianshan Mountains shimmer with a pale blue chill in the morning light. The clouds of the Pamir Plateau drift along the ridges like breath. The waters of Kanas Lake are a green so profound it takes one's breath away. The curves of the desert, at dusk, are drawn out into something soft and golden.
From the aerial height, the grandeur of mountains and rivers rushes forth. Yet when the lens draws near — the tinkle of camel bells as nomads shift pastures, the flecks of light filtering through the Euphrates poplar groves, a nameless wildflower by the shores of Sayram Lake — everything carries a living, breathing warmth.
What moves me most is its unhurried, unhurried cadence. The wind, the melting of snow, the fall of hooves upon the meadow — all are gathered faithfully into the frame, as though carrying the viewer into that vast and open world. It captures not merely scenery, but a way of being: the quiet, unhurried coexistence of humankind and the land. That vastness, that stillness, travels through the screen and settles in the heart.
When it ended, there was only one thought left:
The beauty of Xinjiang deserves to be recorded with such devotion, such tenderness.
This documentary has done so.
